title: Delirious Mania Associated with Autoimmune Gastrothyroidal Syndrome of a Mid-Life Female: The Role of Hashimoto Encephalopathy and a 3-Year Follow-Up including Serum Autoantibody Levels
case_prompt:
A 57-year-old woman reported a year-long history of progressive fatigue, cold intolerance, constipation, and declining concentration attributed to work stress. Over the past four weeks, she developed apathy, mutism, fluctuating confusion, amnesia, disorganization, and urinary incontinence, prompting hospital admission.

On examination she was bradycardic and hypothermic, with dry skin, delayed relaxation of tendon reflexes, myalgias, and a small pericardial effusion. Laboratory tests revealed severe hypothyroidism (high TSH, low free T4), elevated AST and creatine kinase, hypercholesterolemia, and macrocytic anemia despite normal serum vitamins B1, B6, B9, B12, methylmalonic acid, and holotranscobalamin; homocysteine was mildly elevated. Serum anti–thyroid peroxidase antibodies were markedly elevated and anti–TSH receptor antibodies were also elevated; thyroid ultrasound showed gland atrophy.

Brain MRI demonstrated scattered T2-hyperintense white-matter lesions in the temporal lobes and the EEG showed diffuse slowing. CSF analysis revealed elevated protein, S-100 protein, and neuron-specific enolase without pleocytosis or oligoclonal bands; anti–thyroid peroxidase antibodies were detected in CSF. Infectious studies (viral, bacterial, and spirochetal serologies), paraneoplastic and autoimmune synaptic antibody panels, toxicology screens, and systemic immunologic studies were unremarkable. Other limbic encephalopathies, paraneoplastic, infectious, metabolic, or toxic causes were excluded.
diagnostic_reasoning:
1. Severe hypothyroidism–induced encephalopathy considered because of multi-system hypothyroid signs — “Some mental symptoms of the patient can be alternatively explained by severe hypothyroidism (preceding depression, hypoactive delirium, mania, elevated CSF protein, EEG-slowing, and WMH)”.  
2. Rapid thyroid-hormone replacement causing hyperactive delirium and mania — “or rapid adjustment of THRT (hyperactive delirium and mania)”.  
3. Glucocorticoid-induced mania considered but ruled out because psychiatric symptoms improved with high-dose steroids — “A direct influence of glucocorticoid exposure to the development of delirious mania is unlikely because this condition improved during steroid pulse therapy.”  
4. Bipolar disorder considered but unlikely given no personal or family psychiatric history — “Personal and family history of our patient was unremarkable in this regard.”  
5. Other limbic encephalopathies (paraneoplastic, vasculitic, autoimmune synaptic) excluded by negative antibody panels and imaging — “Other forms of limbic encephalopathies that could have been associated with antibodies against intracellular, synaptic, or other cell surface antigenic targets, neoplasm, connective tissue, or vasculitis diseases were excluded.”  
6. Infectious, metabolic, or toxic etiologies excluded by normal CSF cell count, negative microbiology, and normal toxicology — “exclusion of infectious, metabolic, paraneoplastic, or toxic etiologies (by serum, CSF, and brain imaging).”  
7. Vitamin B deficiency excluded by normal levels of B1, B6, B9, B12, methylmalonic acid, and holotranscobalamin — “without laboratory vitamin B deficiency (normal serum levels of vitamins B1, B6, B9, and B12, methylmalonic acid, and holotranscobalamin).”
